headline: Samsung firmware update bricks thousands of refrigerators ahead of major South Korean holiday
summary: A "routine" firmware update for Samsung smart fridges in South Korea caused thousands of units to malfunction, leaving owners with spoiling food just before the Chuseok holiday.
details: An erroneous "routine" firmware update from Samsung has bricked thousands of smart refrigerators in South Korea. The update caused units to get stuck during the process, rendering them inoperable just days before the Chuseok holiday.

Affected customers reported issues like non-functional auto-open features, no interior lights, and rising internal temperatures. Many discovered the problem hours after the update began, with some lamenting food spoilage and failed attempts to reset their units.

The timing is particularly problematic, as Chuseok is a three-day mid-autumn harvest festival where families stock up on food. Delayed service, with technicians unavailable until October, meant significant food loss for many.

Samsung acknowledged the severity, promising restoration by September 24 and deploying emergency on-site services. The company is also reviewing compensation for spoiled food, addressing consumer outrage.

This incident raises questions about the reliability of "smart" home appliances and the risks of software updates. Despite Samsung's plans for AI chips in all appliances, the potential for a faulty update to disable essential devices highlights significant user concerns.

headline_marked: [[Pixel phones broadcast location]] for hours after power-off; here's how to disable it
headline: Pixel phones broadcast location for hours after power-off; here's how to disable it
summary: Google Pixel 8 and newer models can send a low-power Bluetooth signal for hours after shutdown, allowing offline tracking. You can disable this feature while keeping Find Hub active for online tracking.
details: Google Pixel 8 and newer models feature offline tracking, allowing them to send a low-power Bluetooth signal for hours after being powered off. This enables other nearby devices to detect the signal and relay approximate location information to Google's servers.

While this is a useful security feature for locating lost or stolen phones, some users may be uncomfortable with their device remaining detectable after being deliberately turned off. Google states that the location information is end-to-end encrypted.

The option to disable this powered-off tracking is not immediately obvious, despite a brief message appearing during shutdown. It is nested deep within the device's security settings, separate from the main Find Hub controls.

To disable it, navigate to Settings > Security & privacy > Lost device protection > Find Hub > Find your offline devices. Here, you can select "Off" to stop offline tracking, while still allowing Find Hub to function when your phone is on and connected.

A recent Android Canary build further enhances security by preventing Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and mobile data toggling from the lock screen without biometric authentication. This helps prevent a stolen Pixel from being easily disconnected from the internet.

For most users, powered-off finding is a valuable recovery option that significantly increases the chances of finding a lost or stolen device, even if the SIM card is removed. Disabling it is a personal preference, trading off this benefit for complete privacy when powered down.
